en: He was skilled with the white battle-axe,
An expert in warfare,
A mighty one who found the enemy's stratagem,
He was,
Mottled-bodied and very lean,
A servant fit for a hero.
Without fearing this man alone,
With iron ropes and nets,
With ranks of Kanjarkol men,
I shall surround him
And bring him utter torment.
With sixty sorcerers and a thousand champions,
I, the lion, at their head,
Shall stalk the poor man carefully
And pierce him with one overturning thrust.
Is there a mane upon dark water?
While Khan Kongurbay stands,
Is there a khan a tether can reach?
Against the ill-fated Burut,
Will my Zholoy leave anything undone?
If I send him with an order,
Will hairy-soled Tükübay
Not bind and seize
Every one of the handful of Burut?"
Before swaggering Ezkara
Had withdrawn his words,
The many Muslim khans
Had filed past like sheep.
Ezkara of the infidels
Had thoroughly assessed
The Muslim heroes.
There was Kozubek of the Kokon khan;
When he saw Kozubek,
He called him "the lumbering one."
There was Malabek of Margalang;
When he saw Malabek,
He called him "one who capers
Like a foal at the tethering line."
There was fork-bearded Synzhybek of Anzhiyan;
He called him "one who struts
Like a male black crow."
He now knew that the vast black host
Of Muslims had gathered,
And knew that bloodthirsty Manas
Was not there.
My courageous hero Khan Zholoy
Was like a spur of the black mountain.
If Kongurbay truly attacked,
Having come claiming to hold a true feast,
Let them not say there was slaughter
Among the people of Chynmachyn.
Heed what I say, Burut;
Give me what I demand, Burut.
Kökötöy's Maaniker
Is a deep-rooted black racehorse;
This horse borders on the supernatural,
Its tail and mane set it apart,
And it appears suited to us.
It will not tire when ridden scouting,
Nor grow sore when ridden with the baggage train.
It is a beast with wings,
A creature fit for a khan.
Fastening on his mail,
It could circle Beijing five times;
It is a mount heroes would ride!
It has the marks of a racehorse;
Mounted by striving heroes,
It is a beast that could travel Beijing.
Heed my demand, Burut;
Give me Maaniker, Burut!
If you do not give me Maaniker,
If you do not heed what I say,
I will brook no excuses,
I will not eat the meat you have served!
The place I came from is Bakburchun;
I have heard that Kokotoy's Maaniker
Is a peerless racehorse.
I have my Manchu and Chinese people;
If you do not give me Maaniker,
Burut, I have a score to settle with you.
Clad in mail,
He is a steed for heroes to ride.
Wearing a wrist guard,
He is a steed for commanders to ride.
To load him with gold and silver,
To present him to Esen Khan,
Maaniker is a fitting racehorse.
To deck him in precious stones,
To ride him proudly,
Maaniker is a matchless racehorse.
He is a steed worthy
Of the Great Khan of Beijing.
Of the Kalmyks clad in jackets,
He is a steed for the strongest to ride.
Of the stone-bedecked Chinese,
He is a steed for the finest to ride.
This is Kokotoy's memorial feast,
The foremost of great gatherings.
If you do not give me Maaniker,
I have a judgment formed by testing,
And a snare I mean to set.
I will pay no heed to your feast;
Damn you, Burut slave,
I will not rest until I take Maaniker!
Now I will plunder your wealth,
And lay your people waste.
I will spare none of you,
Now I will beat the fury out of you!
On the road through Toorakty-Chylan,
At the hand of mountain-like Joloy,
You inflicted cruel torment,
Destroyed a thousand champions,
And took tea worth a thousand camels.
You committed such a deed;
This outrage of yours remains,
And you cast warriors down dead;
This tyranny of yours remains too.
Agree to these words, Burut,
Without quarreling or making strife;
For the offense committed before,
Give me Maaniker, Burut.
I have words to say;
Burut, I have a score to settle with you.
When, before the Great Khan,
I had received his command,
And loaded gold upon a thousand camels,
Because of you, Burut,
As I went to trade,
You stirred up strife on the steppe,
Slaughtered a thousand champions,
And seized as plunder
The riches borne by a thousand camels.
You committed a grave deed against the Khan;
By doing this too, Burut,
You have become guilty.
To unleash a great tumult,
I set out prepared from Beijing
To plunder you, Burut.
Know my readiness from this:
I have iron armor no bullet can pierce.
To plunder you,
I have an army of twelve tumens,
And a mighty man named Kongurbay.
You swaggering Burut,
I have an answer to exact from you.
If you bristle and strut,
I will seize you at once,
Into a dungeon forty fathoms deep
I will take you away and cast you;
Damn you, dog of a Burut,
Thus will I take my revenge!
I will not stay for this feast of yours;
I will not rest until I take Maaniker.
I will take your steed Maaniker;
I have seen your old man Koshoy.
If you do not give me Maaniker,
I will not leave you alive.
If I unleash my great fury,
Here at this feast of yours
I will raise an uproar,
And water your ravine with blood.
I came wishing to fight,
To make strife where there was none.
From Beijing in Chin-Machin,
Truly venting my rage,
I came wishing to do battle.
Upon Maaniker's back,
Load nothing but gold;
Put an end to the quarrel, Burut,
And present him to me now.
For riding to feasts and celebrations,
For making him prance,
Maaniker is a splendid horse."
As Ezkara spoke,
As he used such force,
Manas, who used to make havoc, was gone—
So God had struck them!
Willow-covered Keng-Kol and broad Talas,
His homeland came to mind;
The joyous leopard Manas,
That hero came to mind.
Ezkara began his speech;
Kokotoy's noble son,
From atop the blue-gray pacer,
Nearly flew off;
The strength left his arms,
And Kokotoy's Bokmurun
Lost heart.
God's sun in the sky grew overcast;
Sixty cares descended upon his head at once.
His wits in disarray,
Without saying a word in reply,
Kokotoy's Bokmurun
Fled away from the people.
To Koshoy, father of the people,
Bokmurun went.
He wept out his grief,
And from his uncle Koshoy
He sought counsel:
"Kokotoy's abundant riches—
Heeding no one's words,
I seem to have come to scatter them.
Humiliation no dog has seen,
I seem to have come to endure.
At the hands of the Black Chinese and Manchus,
In sorrow before my destined death,
I seem to have come to die.
I have come to be beaten
By the panting Kalmyks,
And, saying I would hold a memorial feast,
I have come to let all the people
Be plundered for all time.
A mighty force has come from the Kalmyks, uncle;
When I consider it, all the Manchus have come, uncle.
If I stumble, be my support, uncle;
Be a prop for this mortal soul, uncle!
A khan like Ezkara has appeared, uncle;
His wrath drives the life from me, uncle.
Will the Kyrgyz die at the Kalmyks' hands, uncle?
Will the Chinese divide my people, uncle?
Will they heap tribulation on our heads, uncle?
Will the grim-faced Black Chinese
Raid us and wipe us out, uncle?
Infidels as numerous as ants
Will surely trample us underfoot, uncle?
Will they scatter all four kinds of livestock, uncle?
Will they dig out even the stumps and pass on, uncle?
Will they bind the Muslim heroes
And carry them off to Beijing, uncle?
Will they heap suffering on our heads, uncle?
Will they drive us to their city
And make us slaves, uncle?
Let us submit to what
The Black Kalmyks and Manchus demand, uncle.
So they do not slaughter the people,
They ask for Maaniker; let us give him, uncle.
Let us scatter our countless riches, uncle,
And flee toward Samarkand, uncle!
May your feast be damned—
Can anyone hold a feast as we have, uncle?
Can one prosper after falling
Into the hands of Chinese as numerous as ants, uncle?
He gathered every troubling word;
Maaniker was wealth left by my father,
And he demanded him, uncle.
The moon has turned into darkest night, uncle;
This has become a day of suffering, uncle!
Intoxicated by this wretched wealth,
We came saying we would hold a feast, uncle;
We have chosen torment instead, uncle,
And died before our destined deaths, uncle!
I did not heed my elder's words, uncle;
Now I have fallen into distress, uncle!
I did not heed the wise man's words, uncle;
Coming here saying I would give a feast,
I have fallen into a force beyond reckoning, uncle!
